title: Twenty Nations Propose a Global AI Oversight Body as the US and China Stand Aside, While Trump Confirms US-Iran Talks at the UN
subhead: A coalition of 20 countries and the EU, led from the Finnish president's office, called for a new international institution to police AI just before a Trump-Xi summit — but Washington and Beijing stayed out. In New York, Trump confirmed a 'very good' three-hour US-Iran meeting even as he threatened to annihilate the Islamic Republic.

sections.heading: Twenty Nations Seek a Global AI Watchdog — Without the Two Powers That Matter Most
sections.body:
Twenty countries and the European Union issued a joint declaration on Monday calling for an international institution to set and enforce AI standards, as world leaders gathered for the UN General Assembly. The statement, released through the office of Finnish President Alexander Stubb, urges governments to keep AI under 'human direction, oversight and control', share reports of serious safety incidents, and explore an oversight body that could 'set standards, enable verification, and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed'.

Signatories include Germany, South Africa, Canada, Australia, the UAE and Singapore, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Germany's Friedrich Merz and Turkey's Hakan Fidan among those backing it, according to Al Jazeera. Crucially, the US and China — the world's two leading AI powers — did not join. Washington and Beijing have both rebuffed calls to slow AI development, and the declaration lands days before presidents Trump and Xi are expected to discuss AI at their third summit in under a year at the White House on Thursday.
sections.whyItMatters: The declaration crystallises a split between the states that want AI governed multilaterally and the two powers actually driving its development. With the US and China both absent, the 'global' oversight body would be largely symbolic — unless the Trump-Xi meeting produces a bilateral framework instead, which is the more likely path to binding rules.

sections.heading: At the UN, Trump Threatens Annihilation in One Breath, Negotiates in the Next
sections.body:
The centrepiece of the UNGA session was a study in contradiction. On the floor of the General Assembly, President Trump told world leaders that Iran faced a choice of 'potential greatness or obliteration', saying he could 'annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly'. Minutes of rhetoric apart, Trump told reporters that US officials — including envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — held a 'very good, very productive' three-hour meeting with Iranian leaders, with another session scheduled 'in the very near future'.

Trump signalled a deal could come after November's US congressional elections, insisting that does not factor into his Iran calculus and repeating that 'Iran will never have a nuclear weapon'. Al Jazeera reported an 'air of optimism' among negotiators. Elsewhere in New York, Turkey's Erdogan delivered a blistering attack on Israel's 'genocidal mindset', Qatar's emir called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen and rejected its use as a 'bargaining chip', and both Jordan's King Abdullah and UN chief Antonio Guterres condemned Israeli West Bank settlement expansion.
sections.whyItMatters: After weeks of open war, the public threats and private talks running in parallel mean the US-Iran trajectory now hinges on whether the next meeting converts verbal optimism into a ceasefire — and on the US midterms. The simultaneous UN condemnations of Israel widen the diplomatic isolation the US faces even as it manages the Iran file.

sections.heading: Trump Reportedly Pulls Back From Striking the Houthis as the Battle for Bab al-Mandab Intensifies
sections.body:
In Yemen, the Houthi rebels are fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of the Kahboub Mountains in Taiz and Lahj provinces — heights that overlook the Bab al-Mandeb strait and Mayyun Island, and whose capture would let the Houthis cut the coast off from the remaining government-held south. Renewed hostilities have killed at least 674 people and displaced more than 158,000, Al Jazeera reported, and the Houthi leadership warned the US against direct military involvement.

Against that backdrop, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration prepared air attacks against the Houthis on Sunday after renewed pleas from Riyadh — only for Trump to call them off at the last minute, even as soldiers were loading bombs onto aircraft. Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has repeatedly pressed Washington to join the fight, but the administration has so far rebuffed those requests, while Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi warned Pakistan and Turkiye against joining a Saudi-led escalation.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump's last-minute decision not to strike the Houthis reflects the administration's restraint, or exhaustion, in a widening war. But with the Houthis pressing toward Bab al-Mandeb, the failure to act risks giving the Iran-aligned movement effective control over one of the world's most critical shipping chokepoints.

sections.heading: Xi Purges His Closest Military Ally From the Party
sections.body:
China expelled two of its most senior generals from the Communist Party, state news agency Xinhua reported, for 'seriously violat(ing) political discipline', forming 'cliques and factions' and being 'disloyal and dishonest to the party'. Zhang Youxia — long seen as President Xi Jinping's closest military ally and vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission — and Liu Zhenli, a CMC member and chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department, were removed from the Party after investigations opened in January and dismissal from the military in late August, according to Al Jazeera.

No details of the alleged crimes were provided. The expulsions are the latest chapter in Xi's sweeping anti-corruption campaign, among the largest in modern Chinese history, which previously removed the defence minister and his predecessor in 2024.
sections.whyItMatters: Purging the second-highest military officer breaks a taboo in the PLA's carefully managed hierarchy and concentrates even more control of the armed forces in Xi's hands. It matters strategically because it comes as Beijing weighs its posture toward Taiwan and the US, and as the military leadership undergoes its deepest reshuffle in years.

sections.heading: Russian Strikes Continue as Zelenskyy Arrives for the UN Summit
sections.body:
Overnight missile and drone attacks on several Ukrainian regions killed at least three people just as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in New York for the UN General Assembly, Al Jazeera reported. The strikes underscore that the war on the ground continues unabated even as world leaders gather to discuss it and while Washington and Moscow pursue parallel diplomatic channels.

The UNGA session coincides with the Trump-Xi summit scheduled for Thursday in Washington, where AI is expected to feature alongside the Taiwan question — the subject of a disputed $14 billion US arms sale that Beijing has sharply opposed.
sections.whyItMatters: The persistent Russian strikes highlight the gap between high-level diplomacy in New York and the reality on the front line. With a US-Iran détente uncertain and a Ukraine settlement no closer, the UNGA's crowded agenda reflects a world managing multiple simultaneous crises rather than resolving them.

bottomLine: The day's defining feature was the UN General Assembly, where a 20-nation push for a global AI oversight body landed with the US and China pointedly absent, and where Trump combined a threat to 'annihilate' Iran with confirmation of 'very good' talks that now move to another round. The AI declaration and the Trump-Xi summit that follows will test whether the two AI superpowers can agree on anything, while in Yemen a battle for the heights above Bab al-Mandeb and a last-minute US pullback from striking the Houthis leave the fate of the Red Sea chokepoint unresolved.
